data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's own terms without smuggling in induction, provided it is framed strictly as a methodological rule based on the asymmetry of risk rather than a prediction of future success.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If Popper explicitly stated that acting on corroboration requires an inductive assumption about the uniformity of nature.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the preference for corroborated theories can only be justified by assigning them a higher subjective probability of future success.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 'asymmetry of risk' argument implicitly relies on the premise that past performance indicates future reliability.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Popper distinguishes between the logical status of a theory (which corroboration does not alter regarding probability) and the pragmatic decision of which theory to test or act upon. The mechanism relies on the 'asymmetry of risk': rejecting a well-corroborated theory in favor of a less tested one exposes the agent to a higher risk of immediate falsification without gaining any corresponding increase in informational content or testability. Therefore, choosing the better-corroborated theory is a rational application of the critical method to minimize the chance of error in the present moment, not an inductive inference that the theory will hold true in the future.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
